analysis.one_liner: Restricts high-cost mortgage lenders from charging prepayment penalties, balloon payments, and financed credit insurance fees.
analysis.headline: The Predatory Lending Consumer Protection Act of 2000 never got a vote in the House Banking Committee and died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal rules for high-cost home mortgages, which target borrowers with weak credit and high fees. It would have banned balloon payments, limited prepayment penalties to a short window, barred lenders from financing expensive single-premium credit insurance into the loan, required lenders to verify a borrower's actual income before lending, banned forced arbitration clauses, and made Wall Street buyers of these loans legally responsible for the lenders' abuses. It also let borrowers sue for up to three years and raised penalties for violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners, especially older and lower-income borrowers who take out high-cost mortgages or are targeted by home-improvement loan scams. They would keep more home equity, face fewer foreclosure traps, and have stronger legal remedies.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits all balloon payments on high-cost mortgages and limits prepayment penalties to the first 24 months, so borrowers who sell or refinance are not charged for escaping the loan [S2][S3]
Requires lenders to verify each borrower's income and ability to repay without counting home equity, attacking the practice of lending against equity the borrower cannot afford to service [S2][S3]
Bans financing single-premium credit life and disability insurance into the loan and caps the points and fees a lender can finance, blocking charges that strip equity at closing [S2][S3]

Bans mandatory arbitration clauses and makes buyers of these mortgages liable for the original lender's misconduct on home-improvement loans, giving borrowers access to court and a target with real assets [S2][S3]

Extends the statute of limitations for violations from one to three years and raises civil penalties per violation from $2,000 to $10,000, with class-action liability up to 2% of the creditor's net worth [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Subprime and high-cost mortgage lenders, mortgage brokers, and sellers of single-premium credit insurance, whose fee income and volume would shrink; some marginal borrowers may have found fewer lenders willing to extend high-cost credit.

drawbacks.text: Tight ability-to-repay rules and fee caps shrink the supply of credit to borrowers with poor credit histories, who might lose access to any home loan rather than a predatory one [S3]

Compliance costs fall on all high-cost originators, including smaller community and consumer lenders, and lenders might steer marginal applicants just under the thresholds rather than improve loan terms [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target documented abuses — equity stripping, financed insurance, forced arbitration — that routinely cost borrowers their homes, while the cost side is a smaller and less certain reduction in credit availability to subprime borrowers. The bill still permitted high-cost lending with a prepayment-penalty window and monthly-pay insurance, so it regulated rather than eliminated the market. On balance the gains to borrowers' home equity and legal rights outweigh the credit-supply cost, though lenders' access-to-credit objection was real.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking and Financial Services Committee and its financial institutions subcommittee on the day it was introduced, neither ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. John LaFalce introduced the bill on April 12, 2000 with nine original cosponsors including Reps. Vento, Frank, Kanjorski, Maloney, and Gutierrez [S1][S3]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services and to its Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit [S5]
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind after the day of referral [S5]
The bill gathered 18 cosponsors, all Democrats, before the 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001 [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost mortgage lenders, mortgage brokers, and single-premium credit insurance sellers avoided new restrictions; their fees, penalties, and insurance premiums continued to be charged to borrowers.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and all 18 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support, and the Republican-controlled Banking Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill's core restrictions — no balloon payments, capped financed fees, income verification, no discretionary acceleration — directly cut the fee and rate income that high-cost lending generates, much of which comes from borrowers at risk of losing their homes.

industries.industry: Sellers of single-premium credit life and disability insurance
industries.note: The bill bans financing a single upfront premium for credit insurance into a mortgage, eliminating a product sold almost entirely through lenders that often costs more than any benefit it delivers.
All broker compensation, direct or indirect, would count toward the points-and-fees cap, shrinking broker payouts on high-cost loans.

industries.industry: Buyers of high-cost mortgages in the secondary market
industries.note: Assignees and holders would inherit the borrower's claims and defenses on home-improvement-financed loans, raising the risk of holding these mortgages.
